questions.question: Substituting $x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ into $x^{(n)}+a_{n-1}x^{(n-1)}+\dots+a_0x=0$ (constant real $a_k$) gives $p(r)\,\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ with $p(r)=r^n+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\dots+a_0$. Why is $\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ a solution exactly when $p(r)=0$?
options: Because every derivative of $\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ equals $\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ itself
Because $p(r)=0$ makes each derivative $x^{(k)}(t)$ vanish separately
Because $\mathrm{e}^{rt}=1$ at $t=0$, which fixes the value of $r$

questions.question: Can the characteristic-equation method, which substitutes $x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ with a constant $r$, be applied to the linear equation $x''(t)+t\,x(t)=0$, whose coefficient of $x$ depends on $t$, and why?
options: No: $(r^2+t)\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ is not identically zero for any constant $r$
Yes: the characteristic equation is $r^2+t=0$, so $r=\pm\sqrt{-t}$
Yes, but only on the interval $t>0$ where the coefficient is positive
Yes, after freezing the coefficient $t$ at the initial time $t_0$

questions.question: A homogeneous linear equation of order $4$ with constant real coefficients has characteristic roots $2$ (double) and $1\pm i$. How many real solution functions does the root method produce?
options: $2$: one per distinct root value, $\mathrm{e}^{2t}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{t}\cos t$
$6$: two real functions for each of the three distinct roots

questions.question: With $y_1=x$, $y_2=x'$, the equation $x''-5x'+6x=0$ becomes $\boldsymbol{y}'=A\boldsymbol{y}$ with companion matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-6&5\end{pmatrix}$. What are the eigenvalues of $A$?
What is the characteristic equation of the constant-coefficient equation $2x''(t)-3x'(t)+x(t)=0$?
The equation $x''(t)+4x'(t)+4x(t)=0$ has the double characteristic root $-2$. Which pair of functions is a pair of linearly independent solutions?
The characteristic roots of $x''(t)+4x'(t)+13x(t)=0$ are nonreal. Which family of real functions solves the equation for all constants $c_1,c_2$?
Which three functions solve the third-order equation $x'''(t)-x'(t)=0$ and come from its characteristic roots?

For a real constant-coefficient equation with characteristic roots $\alpha\pm i\beta$, $\beta\neq0$, the complex function $\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha+i\beta)t}=\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}(\cos\beta t+i\sin\beta t)$ is a solution. Why are $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t$ and $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t$ real solutions?
options: Because $\cos\beta t$ and $\sin\beta t$ are periodic, like the oscillation
Because real coefficients act on real and imaginary parts separately
Because $\alpha$ alone is a characteristic root, so $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}$ solves it
Because $|\mathrm{e}^{i\beta t}|=1$, so the complex factor can be dropped

questions.question: A third-order equation $x'''+a_2x''+a_1x'+a_0x=0$ with real constants $a_k$ has $2+3i$ as a characteristic root. What follows about the other two roots?
options: $2-3i$ is a root, and the remaining root is real
$2-3i$ is a root, and the remaining root is nonreal as well
$2-3i$ need not be a root, since only $2+3i$ was given
$-2+3i$ is a root, by the symmetry of the roots

questions.question: For which of these constant-coefficient equations is $x(t)=t\mathrm{e}^{t}$ a solution?
The function $\mathrm{e}^{-t}\cos2t$ solves a second-order equation $x''+ax'+bx=0$ with real constants $a,b$. Which equation is it?
Sampling a continuous-time mode $\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ at integer times $t=0,1,2,\dots$ gives a discrete-time mode $\lambda^t$. If $r=\ln3$ is a characteristic root, which discrete mode corresponds to it?
For a homogeneous linear equation of order at least $2$ with constant coefficients and characteristic polynomial $p$, which statement about exponential solutions is correct?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ solves it iff $p(r)=0$, so every solution is some $c\mathrm{e}^{rt}$
$\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ solves it whenever $p'(r)=0$, the critical points of $p$
$\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ solves it iff $p(r)=0$, and $t\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ solves it iff $p(r)=0$
$\mathrm{e}^{rt}$ solves it iff $p(r)=0$, but not every solution is some $c\mathrm{e}^{rt}$

questions.question: For the roots $\alpha\pm \mathrm{i}\beta$ ($\beta\neq0$) of a real characteristic equation, $\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha+\mathrm{i}\beta)t}$ gives the real solutions $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t$ and $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t$. What do the real and imaginary parts of $\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha-\mathrm{i}\beta)t}$ add?
options: Two further functions, so the pair contributes four real solutions
The functions $\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}\cos\beta t$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}\sin\beta t$
Nothing new: they are $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t$ and $-\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t$
Nothing, because $\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha-\mathrm{i}\beta)t}$ is not a solution

questions.question: The fourth-order equation $x''''+2x''+x=0$ has characteristic polynomial $r^4+2r^2+1=(r^2+1)^2$. Which four functions are independent solutions?
options: $\cos t,\ \sin t,\ t^2\cos t,\ t^2\sin t$
$\cos t,\ \sin t,\ t\cos t,\ t\sin t$

questions.question: For which real values of the constant $k$ does the equation $x''+k\,x'+9x=0$ have nonreal characteristic roots, so that its real solutions contain $\cos$ and $\sin$ factors?
